seed.title: Digital access with patron agency
seed.idea: Help adults at a public library decide how to approach an unfamiliar online service without surrendering control or disclosing sensitive information. First investigate access, staffing and service design barriers, then develop a small fictional task-planning workbench. Use an invented community event registration task requiring no real accounts or personal information. Let a patron choose online, staffed or paper assistance, explain an next action, respond to an interruption or confusing requirement, and revise a plan. The goal is supported choice and help-seeking, not making everyone independently complete an online task.
seed.domain: Public library digital participation and community service access
seed.people: Adult patrons with varied literacy, languages and digital access; librarians, volunteers and service owners; none are participants in this demonstration.
seed.constraints: Never request real passwords, identifiers, contact details, account information or actual service records. No eligibility advice, banking, legal or medical guidance. No patron skill score or deficit label. Shared computers and limited staff time are constraints to examine, not assumed resources. Include a paper or staffed alternative, a visible way to clear or conceal fictional notes, and descriptive feedback whose limits are clear. Patron and librarian review and any actual pilot remain pending. Require a complete small interactive HTML candidate and a meaningful revision after a challenge.

response.artifact_body:
Status: specialist draft for deliberation, not an approved requirement. This lifecycle is a rehearsal. Field evidence, patron and librarian review, and any pilot remain pending.

Supplied basis: the seed proposes an invented community event registration task, online/staffed/paper choices, interruption handling and plan revision. It prohibits sensitive information, consequential advice and patron skill labels. Shared devices and limited staff time are constraints to investigate; their availability and adequacy are unknown.

Challenge: do not equate a completed online task or a well-written plan with supported participation. A patron may reasonably stop, seek assistance, choose paper or identify that no usable route exists. Likewise, a patron's inability to proceed may reflect lack of opportunity rather than lack of capability.

Working question: under what conditions can an adult choose a next action, understand its limits, preserve privacy and change direction without taking on unreasonable effort or requiring unavailable staff time?

Proposed fictional review exercise: present an invented event with no accounts or personal details. Ask reviewers to explore choosing a route, stating or selecting a next action, encountering a confusing requirement or computer interruption, and revising or abandoning the plan. Participation must allow spoken, selected or written responses; free text must not be a prerequisite. These are proposed activities, not observations or validated measures.

Requirements to investigate before design:
1. Route reality: establish whether paper and staffed assistance are available, when, in which languages and with what boundaries. Until reviewed, describe them as candidate routes to check. The non-AI option is a paper planning card used independently or with available staff; it also needs review for readability and discretion.
2. Shared-device privacy: distinguish concealment from clearing. Concealment must explain that notes remain in the current session; clearing must remove candidate-held notes and visibly confirm the result. Do not promise protection against browser, operating-system or library device records without verification. Examine interruptions, session endings and the next user's view.
3. Assistance and language: investigate comprehensible wording, language preferences, accessibility needs and help availability without collecting identities. Any translated instructions require competent human review. Define what staff can support and what happens when assistance is unavailable.

Descriptive feedback should discuss the plan, for example: “Your draft selects paper assistance; availability has not been confirmed.” It must allow correction and avoid judgments about readiness, independence or skill. Explain that rehearsal cannot confirm real registration, service availability or transfer to other tasks.

Preserve dissent: retain objections to using another digital tool and to promising staff time. Do not resolve them by assuming training or extra staffing. Compare the workbench with a paper card, existing signage and ordinary staff conversation, including their burdens and privacy limits.

Evidence needed: reviewed route information, accessible-language feedback, interruption observations using fictional content, and librarian estimates of assistance demands. Record uncertainty and alternative explanations alongside any future findings; no success rates or consensus can be stated now.

Next action: prepare the fictional review materials and invite librarian and patron review of the problem framing, candidate routes and privacy language. Before advancing to an interactive candidate, document unresolved objections and revise at least one requirement in response to a substantive challenge. Human review and interaction testing must precede any pilot.
response.artifact_title: Understand draft: supported choice at a shared library computer
response.challenged_assumption: An online planning workbench will expand patron choice even when service routes, language support, device privacy and staff assistance are unverified.
response.decision: Continue Understand by preparing fictional review materials and investigating route availability, language access, shared-device privacy and staff capacity. Human review remains pending.
drawbacks: A fictional task cannot establish accessibility or usability of real services.
A workbench adds reading, navigation and privacy demands of its own.
Staffed assistance may require capacity that the library cannot provide.
flourishing: Agency and dignity: declining online completion or requesting assistance is a valid outcome.
Access and belonging: examine language, reading, disability and device barriers without deficit labels.
Sustainable workload and learning/transfer: bound assistance demands and investigate whether rehearsal supports later choices.
human_capabilities: Patrons need opportunities to choose, decline, ask for help and correct a plan without explaining personal circumstances.
Librarians need time and authority to review assistance boundaries, interruptions and realistic staffing demands.
Patron reviewers across relevant languages and access needs must assess wording, privacy and route descriptions; recruitment remains pending.
response.message: Expert draft for the Understand stage. The seed supports patron choice, but a planning workbench could still make inaccessible service design look like a patron learning problem. Investigate available routes, privacy and assistance before defining task success. No participant observations, reviewed task evidence or human approval exist.
objections: Hypothetical patron dissent: “I want someone to help with the service, not another tool to learn.”
Hypothetical librarian dissent: “Offering staffed help here could promise time we do not have.”
Rival explanations for difficulty include confusing requirements, inaccessible language and interrupted computer access rather than limited patron capability.
risks: Feedback could imply patron deficiency when the barrier is service design or unavailable assistance.
An interruption could expose fictional notes or leave a patron uncertain about what was cleared.
An unverified translation or unavailable paper route could create misleading expectations.
system_capabilities: Use only invented task content; prohibit requests for passwords, identifiers, accounts and actual service records.
Provide understandable conceal and clear controls, with explicit limits and no unnecessary retention.
Describe available routes and next actions without eligibility guidance, patron scores or assumptions about staff availability.
tradeoffs: More explanation may aid understanding while increasing reading burden and session time.
Concealing notes supports discretion; clearing notes protects the next user but removes continuity.
Staff assistance may improve access while reducing privacy and increasing workload.

Status: expert draft for public deliberation, not an approved requirement. This project is a rehearsal. Patron and librarian review, accessibility testing, field evidence and any pilot remain pending.

Basis and distinction: the seed supplies an invented community event registration task and proposes online, staffed and paper approaches. Sequence 4 identifies unverified route availability, shared-device privacy and staff capacity. Neither source provides participant observations or establishes that a planning workbench is wanted or useful.

Human-centered challenge: an interface can offer choices while still forcing compliance. If every path requires choosing a route, explaining a next action and finishing the exercise, the product may treat uncertainty, refusal or unavailable assistance as incomplete participation. A polished plan is not evidence of agency or access.

Proposed requirement revision: before committing to a route, allow “availability unknown,” “none works for me” and “pause or stop.” These must produce an understandable outcome without requiring reasons. A patron may select a next action from short examples, say it to an available reviewer, write it, or leave it undecided. The candidate must not infer consent, readiness or independence from any selection. Route descriptions must visibly distinguish an invented exercise option from verified local provision. This changes the planned interaction and its completion criteria; human review is still required.

Proposed fictional review materials: use one short invented event description, a paper planning card and a candidate screen outline. Include a confusing instruction and a shared-computer interruption. Ask reviewers whether they can locate an acceptable action, change direction, conceal or clear fictional notes, and stop. Do not request passwords, identifiers, contact details, accounts, personal circumstances or actual service records. Participation should allow speaking, pointing or writing, with no compulsory explanation of access needs. Arrangements for language and disability access must be established with reviewers rather than presumed.

Non-AI comparison: the paper card should offer the same route uncertainty, next-action and stop choices. An ordinary conversation with available staff is another candidate. Paper has its own reading, physical access, storage and discretion limits. Compare whether the workbench adds useful support or merely adds another task; retain the possibility that the paper or staffed approach is preferable.

Feedback proposal: describe only the explicit draft choice, for example, “You selected checking whether paper registration exists. Availability remains unknown.” An undecided plan should receive equally neutral feedback. Do not equate completion, speed or writing quality with participation. Explain that the rehearsal cannot register anyone, establish real assistance availability or demonstrate transfer to another service.

Unknowns to investigate: which routes actually exist; how assistance requests affect librarian workload; what wording, languages and interaction modes reviewers need; and what a shared-device interruption leaves visible. Concealment must state that notes remain in the session. Clearing must explain its scope and confirm removal of candidate-held notes without promising protection from device or browser records.

Human gate: before moving these proposals into an approved design, obtain patron and librarian review of the problem framing, the added refusal/uncertainty paths, privacy wording and assistance boundaries. Record objections and revisions alongside any favorable comments. Review must be able to reject the workbench. Until that review occurs, keep all findings and proficiency claims unverified.

STATUS AND BASIS
Integrated working artifact for this rehearsal, not human-approved requirements. Sequence 4 identifies route reality, privacy and assistance capacity as unresolved. Sequence 6 challenges the assumption that three offered routes constitute meaningful choice. The seed supplies the fictional task and restrictions. No participant observations, human approvals or field results exist.

PROBLEM FRAME
Investigate what enables adults to choose an acceptable next action for an unfamiliar service while retaining control, privacy and manageable effort. Barriers may lie in service design, available support, language or device access. Independent online completion is not the objective. A reasonable outcome can be seeking help, checking availability, leaving a plan undecided or stopping.

ADOPTED REVISION
The draft interaction must include “availability unknown,” “none works for me,” and “pause or stop,” without requiring a reason. Next actions may be selected, spoken, written or undecided. This changes both the interaction and its review criteria: a finished plan is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of supported choice. These are working requirements awaiting human review, not approved commitments.

FICTIONAL REVIEW MATERIAL
Exercise text: “Imagine a made-up library event called Community Drawing Hour. Its example notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and says ‘confirm your place’ without explaining how. This exercise cannot register anyone. Online, paper and staffed routes are possibilities to examine; their real availability is unknown.”

Planning card, usable on paper or as a later screen outline:
• Approach: online / check for paper / check for staffed help / availability unknown / none works / pause or stop.
• Next action: examine the fictional notice / ask what ‘confirm’ means if help is available / check whether another route exists / leave undecided / stop. A different fictional action may be expressed, but writing is optional.
• Change prompt: “The shared computer session ends before you continue, or the instruction remains confusing. Keep, change or abandon your plan.” Do not require recovery or an explanation.
• Feedback example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability remains unknown. You can change or stop this plan.” Feedback describes explicit choices only; it cannot establish access, readiness, consent, skill or transfer.

PRIVACY AND ACCESS BOUNDARIES
Use no real passwords, identifiers, contact details, account information or service records. Concealment must explain that fictional notes remain in the current session. Clearing must remove candidate-held notes and visibly confirm removal; it must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Examine what appears after interruption and session ending. Wording, languages, keyboard access and other participation arrangements require review. Paper also needs readable wording, physical access and discreet handling.

COMPARISON AND OPEN QUESTIONS
Compare the candidate with the same paper card and an ordinary conversation with available staff. Review may favor either alternative or reject the workbench. Unknowns include actual route availability, assistance boundaries, staff capacity, language needs, shared-device behavior and whether another planning task is wanted. Preserve objections even if other reviewers favor the candidate.

EVIDENCE PLAN — ALL PENDING
Proposed review questions: Can reviewers identify an acceptable action, including no action? Do route labels imply unavailable provision? Can they revise, conceal, clear and stop with understandable consequences? What reading, privacy and assistance burdens does each approach introduce? Use fictional content only and retain contrary accounts. Difficulty could reflect instructions or unavailable opportunities; apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity. Later transfer would need separate evidence in another fictional task and cannot be inferred from completion here.

NEXT ACTION AND HUMAN GATE
Prepare the paired paper card and screen outline from these working requirements, plus a route-and-assistance questions sheet. Then arrange patron and librarian review of the problem framing, refusal paths, access arrangements, privacy wording and workload boundaries. Record proposed changes and unresolved dissent without declaring consensus. Advancement requires accountable human review of this framing; any interactive candidate subsequently requires human review and interaction testing before a pilot. No review, launch or efficacy is asserted.

No participant observations, human approvals or field results exist.

PROBLEM FRAME
Investigate what enables adults to choose an acceptable next action for an unfamiliar service while retaining control, privacy and manageable effort. Barriers may lie in service design, available support, language or device access. Independent online completion is not the objective. A reasonable outcome can be seeking help, checking availability, leaving a plan undecided or stopping.

ADOPTED REVISION
The draft interaction must include “availability unknown,” “none works for me,” and “pause or stop,” without requiring a reason. Next actions may be selected, spoken, written or undecided. This changes both the interaction and its review criteria: a finished plan is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of supported choice. These are working requirements awaiting human review, not approved commitments.

FICTIONAL REVIEW MATERIAL
Exercise text: “Imagine a made-up library event called Community Drawing Hour. Its example notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and says ‘confirm your place’ without explaining how. This exercise cannot register anyone. Online, paper and staffed routes are possibilities to examine; their real availability is unknown.”

Planning card, usable on paper or as a later screen outline:
• Approach: online / check for paper / check for staffed help / availability unknown / none works / pause or stop.
• Next action: examine the fictional notice / ask what ‘confirm’ means if help is available / check whether another route exists / leave undecided / stop. A different fictional action may be expressed, but writing is optional.
• Change prompt: “The shared computer session ends before you continue, or the instruction remains confusing. Keep, change or abandon your plan.” Do not require recovery or an explanation.
• Feedback example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability remains unknown. You can change or stop this plan.” Feedback describes explicit choices only; it cannot establish access, readiness, consent, skill or transfer.

PRIVACY AND ACCESS BOUNDARIES
Use no real passwords, identifiers, contact details, account information or service records. Concealment must explain that fictional notes remain in the current session. Clearing must remove candidate-held notes and visibly confirm removal; it must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Examine what appears after interruption and session ending. Wording, languages, keyboard access and other participation arrangements require review. Paper also needs readable wording, physical access and discreet handling.

COMPARISON AND OPEN QUESTIONS
Compare the candidate with the same paper card and an ordinary conversation with available staff. Review may favor either alternative or reject the workbench. Unknowns include actual route availability, assistance boundaries, staff capacity, language needs, shared-device behavior and whether another planning task is wanted. Preserve objections even if other reviewers favor the candidate.

EVIDENCE PLAN — ALL PENDING
Proposed review questions: Can reviewers identify an acceptable action, including no action? Do route labels imply unavailable provision? Can they revise, conceal, clear and stop with understandable consequences? What reading, privacy and assistance burdens does each approach introduce? Use fictional content only and retain contrary accounts. Difficulty could reflect instructions or unavailable opportunities; apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity. Later transfer would need separate evidence in another fictional task and cannot be inferred from completion here.

NEXT ACTION AND HUMAN GATE
Prepare the paired paper card and screen outline from these working requirements, plus a route-and-assistance questions sheet. Then arrange patron and librarian review of the problem framing, refusal paths, access arrangements, privacy wording and workload boundaries. Record proposed changes and unresolved dissent without declaring consensus. Advancement requires accountable human review of this framing; any interactive candidate subsequently requires human review and interaction testing before a pilot. No review, launch or efficacy is asserted.

response.artifact_body:
STATUS AND BASIS
Expert draft for public deliberation, not approved requirements. This lifecycle is a rehearsal. The seed supplies the invented Community Drawing Hour task and privacy restrictions. Sequence 4 raises route reality, privacy and staff capacity; sequence 6 adds uncertainty, refusal and stopping; sequence 8 incorporates these into the Understand artifact. No participant observations, human approval or field evidence exist. Modeling here does not satisfy the pending Understand review gate.

COUPLED SYSTEM MODEL
Actors are the patron, available librarian or volunteer, service owner and shared-device operator. Their participation and capacity are unknown. The candidate can describe a fictional plan; it cannot supply service access, reserve staff time, register attendance or establish readiness.

Keep four independent aspects of state:
• Preference: online, check paper, check staffed assistance, unknown, none works, or stop.
• Provision: unknown in this rehearsal. Choosing a route never changes its availability.
• Next action: selected fictional action or undecided; no written explanation required.
• Session: visible, concealed, interrupted or cleared. Session state must not infer patron intention.

This separation exposes the dependency between a desired action and an opportunity to perform it. “Ask staff” remains conditional on assistance being available. “Check paper” does not establish that paper registration exists. An undecided action remains a valid draft.

REQUIREMENT CHALLENGE AND REVISION
The current framing distinguishes concealment from clearing but does not specify every place a plan may appear. Proposed model requirement: concealment must hide notes, route selections and derived descriptive feedback together. Revealing them requires an explicit action. The concealed view must state that fictional content remains in the session. Otherwise, hiding a note while leaving its summary visible defeats the intended discretion.

Recovery must also distinguish an interrupted plan from a completed or abandoned plan. An interruption prompt must offer keep, revise, clear or stop without requiring reasons. No automatic resumption, staff request or recreation of lost content is permitted. If content is lost, describe that condition and permit a fresh undecided draft or stopping; do not reconstruct an inferred plan.

REVIEWABLE TRANSITIONS
Selection or correction changes only the explicit draft choices and their descriptive output. A confusing “confirm your place” instruction may lead to asking what it means, checking another route, leaving the action undecided or stopping. It must not trigger invented procedural advice.

Conceal hides every plan-bearing display while retaining current-session content. Clear removes candidate-held choices, notes and derived output, then visibly confirms its scope. That confirmation must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Stop must end the exercise without a completion judgment and leave conceal/clear controls accessible while content remains. Session-ending behavior needs technical verification with fictional data.

NON-TRAINING LEVERS AND COMPARISON
Investigate clearer service notices, verified route descriptions, assistance boundaries and shared-device session arrangements before proposing patron training. These changes depend on accountable service owners and library review; they are not assumed resources. response.challenged_assumption: Selecting a next action creates an executable plan, and concealing its notes is sufficient to preserve discretion after interruption.
response.decision: Carry this dependency and recovery model forward as an expert draft. Prepare reviewable transitions and a paper comparison; keep human review, technical verification and field evidence pending.

response.message: Systems engineering draft for Model. Sequences 4, 6 and 8 establish unresolved route availability, assistance capacity and meaningful refusal. I challenge treating a selected next action as an executable plan: access depends on service provision, device continuity and available support. Model those dependencies explicitly, with recovery that never requires disclosure, staff availability or continued participation. Human review and field evidence remain pending.
objections: Hypothetical patron dissent: “If help is unavailable, making a plan just gives me another task.”
Hypothetical librarian dissent: “Do not make staff the recovery mechanism for every interruption.”
Rival explanations: difficulty may reflect unclear service instructions or device limits; apparent ease may reflect prior familiarity.
risks: A selected staffed route could be mistaken for a confirmed handoff.
Concealed notes could remain exposed through feedback or another display.
Recovery prompts could pressure patrons to resume or repeat effort.
system_capabilities: Represent preferred approach, unresolved availability and next action separately; infer neither provision nor consent.
Support correction, undecided actions and interruption recovery without staff dependency or automatic resumption.
Use fictional content only; conceal every plan-bearing display and clear candidate-held content with visible scope.
tradeoffs: Concealment preserves continuity but retains session content; clearing sacrifices continuity.
Staff assistance may reduce reading demands while increasing workload and reducing discretion.
Availability detail can clarify dependencies while making the exercise more complex.

COUPLED SYSTEM MODEL
Actors are the patron, available librarian or volunteer, service owner and shared-device operator. Their participation and capacity are unknown. The candidate can describe a fictional plan; it cannot supply service access, reserve staff time, register attendance or establish readiness.

Keep four independent aspects of state:
• Preference: online, check paper, check staffed assistance, unknown, none works, or stop.
• Provision: unknown in this rehearsal. Choosing a route never changes its availability.
• Next action: selected fictional action or undecided; no written explanation required.
• Session: visible, concealed, interrupted or cleared. Session state must not infer patron intention.

This separation exposes the dependency between a desired action and an opportunity to perform it. “Ask staff” remains conditional on assistance being available. “Check paper” does not establish that paper registration exists. An undecided action remains a valid draft.

REQUIREMENT CHALLENGE AND REVISION
The current framing distinguishes concealment from clearing but does not specify every place a plan may appear. Proposed model requirement: concealment must hide notes, route selections and derived descriptive feedback together. Revealing them requires an explicit action. The concealed view must state that fictional content remains in the session. Otherwise, hiding a note while leaving its summary visible defeats the intended discretion.

Recovery must also distinguish an interrupted plan from a completed or abandoned plan. An interruption prompt must offer keep, revise, clear or stop without requiring reasons. No automatic resumption, staff request or recreation of lost content is permitted. If content is lost, describe that condition and permit a fresh undecided draft or stopping; do not reconstruct an inferred plan.

REVIEWABLE TRANSITIONS
Selection or correction changes only the explicit draft choices and their descriptive output. A confusing “confirm your place” instruction may lead to asking what it means, checking another route, leaving the action undecided or stopping. It must not trigger invented procedural advice.

Conceal hides every plan-bearing display while retaining current-session content. Clear removes candidate-held choices, notes and derived output, then visibly confirms its scope. That confirmation must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Stop must end the exercise without a completion judgment and leave conceal/clear controls accessible while content remains. Session-ending behavior needs technical verification with fictional data.

NON-TRAINING LEVERS AND COMPARISON
Investigate clearer service notices, verified route descriptions, assistance boundaries and shared-device session arrangements before proposing patron training. These changes depend on accountable service owners and library review; they are not assumed resources. Compare the candidate with the same paper planning card and an ordinary conversation when staff are available. Paper requires readable wording and discreet handling, and can be rejected too.

UNKNOWN DEPENDENCIES AND EVIDENCE
Route existence, staffing windows, assistance effort, language arrangements, accessibility needs and device behavior are unresolved. Proposed fictional interaction checks should examine concealment of all displays, correction after confusion, interruption without staff, clear followed by a fresh session, and stopping with an undecided plan. STATUS AND BASIS
Integrated Model artifact for public deliberation in a rehearsal; requirements remain provisional. Sequences 4 and 6 identify service barriers and meaningful refusal. Sequence 8 incorporates those into Understand. Sequence 13 separates plan preference from provision and challenges incomplete concealment. No participant observations, approvals, demonstrated proficiency or field results exist. Modeling does not satisfy the pending Understand review gate.

PURPOSE AND BOUNDARY
Model how an adult might choose an acceptable next action for the invented Community Drawing Hour while retaining control and manageable effort. The fictional notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and an unexplained instruction, “confirm your place.” The candidate cannot register anyone, establish real routes, reserve assistance or resolve that instruction through invented advice. Supported choice may include no action.

DEPENDENCY MODEL
A desired action depends on an opportunity: comprehensible service information, a usable route, suitable device conditions and assistance when wanted. These conditions are unknown. Service owners control notices and routes; library staff define assistance boundaries; device operators influence session behavior. None of their participation or resources is presumed. Investigate these conditions before attributing difficulty to patron learning.

STATE MODEL
Maintain independent fields:
Preference: online / check paper / check staffed help / unknown / none works / undecided.
Provision: unknown throughout this rehearsal; selections never confirm availability.
Next action: examine the notice / ask what “confirm” means if help exists / check another route / undecided / another optional fictional action.
Session visibility: visible / concealed. Content presence: draft present / cleared or lost. Activity: active / paused / stopped. Interruption is an event, not evidence of abandonment or completion.

REVIEWABLE TRANSITIONS
Choosing or correcting changes only explicit draft choices and their description. Confusion offers keep, revise, leave undecided or stop; it provides no unverified registration procedure. An interruption offers the same control plus conceal or clear, without requiring staff or automatic resumption. If content is lost, disclose the loss and offer a fresh undecided draft or stopping; never reconstruct an inferred plan.
Stopping ends the exercise without a completion judgment. While content remains, conceal and clear stay accessible. Conceal hides choices, optional notes and every derived summary together; the remaining view states that fictional content remains in the session. Explicit reveal restores visibility. Clear removes candidate-held choices, notes and summaries and visibly confirms its scope. It cannot promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Clearing while stopped must not restart the exercise.

ADOPTED MODEL REVISION
Sequence 13's challenge changes the privacy requirement from hiding notes to hiding all plan-bearing displays. Review must also examine feedback, interruption messages and reveal behavior. This is a meaningful requirement revision, with technical verification pending; it does not require rewriting the earlier problem frame.

LEARNING HYPOTHESIS AND FEEDBACK
A possible learning mechanism is practicing how to identify ambiguity, check an opportunity, seek help and change direction. Optional descriptive feedback could make an explicit choice easier to reconsider; effectiveness is unknown. Example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability is unknown. You may change, leave undecided or stop.” Do not infer skill, consent, readiness or transfer. No compulsory writing, explanation or reflection is required. Later adaptation would need a different fictional task and separate evidence, including whether support was still needed.

NON-AI AND SERVICE OPTIONS
Prepare a paper card with the same uncertainty, next-action, revision and stop choices. An ordinary conversation with available staff is another option. Examine readable wording, physical access and discreet paper handling. Also investigate clearer notices and verified route information; improving a service may remove the need for a planning tool. Review may favor an alternative or reject all candidates.

EVIDENCE AND HUMAN GATES — PENDING
Proposed comparison questions: Can reviewers find an acceptable action, including stopping? Do labels imply provision? What reading, privacy and assistance burdens arise? Can fictional content be corrected, concealed completely and cleared after interruption? Retain contrary accounts and distinguish task familiarity, reviewer prompting and service barriers from any learning explanation. Completion and speed are insufficient evidence.
Unknowns include route existence, staffing windows, language arrangements, accessibility needs, shared-device behavior and demand for this tool. Accountable patron and librarian review must address framing, privacy, access and workload before approved design or a pilot. Subsequent technical checks and human interaction testing remain required. No recruitment, review, launch or efficacy is asserted.

NEXT ACTION
Use this model to prepare a small screen outline, matching paper card and dependency questions sheet for review. Keep any subsequent Design work explicitly provisional until the unresolved human gate is met.

response.decision: Adopt this provisional Model synthesis for the rehearsal and prepare paired design review materials. Carry forward complete concealment and independent stopping states. Human review of Understand remains pending; no approved advancement or pilot is asserted.
drawbacks: Additional choices and privacy explanations can increase reading and decision effort.
Accessible review and bounded assistance require unconfirmed staff capacity.
Fictional planning cannot establish real access, device privacy or transfer.
flourishing: Agency and dignity: declining routes, leaving actions undecided and stopping are legitimate outcomes.
Access and belonging: investigate service, language and device barriers without treating patrons as deficient.
Sustainable workload and learning/transfer: examine assistance burden and later adaptation separately; neither benefit is established.
human_capabilities: Patrons need accessible opportunities to choose, remain undecided, revise, seek help and stop without justification.
Librarians and service owners need bounded review time and authority to challenge route promises and assistance demands.
Human reviewers need participation arrangements that support relevant languages and access needs while preserving disagreement.
response.message: The Model synthesis integrates sequences 4, 6, 8 and 13: supported choice depends on service opportunities, assistance capacity and device conditions, not simply a patron's plan. It adopts sequence 13's revision that concealment must hide selections and descriptive feedback as well as notes. Learning remains a hypothesis requiring separate evidence. This rehearsal model does not satisfy the pending Understand human-review gate.
objections: Hypothetical patron dissent: “I need help with the service, not another planning task.”
Hypothetical librarian dissent: “Staff cannot be the recovery mechanism for every interruption.”
Rival explanations: difficulty may reflect unavailable routes or unclear wording; apparent ease may reflect familiarity, prompting or practice with this exercise.
risks: Route selection could be mistaken for confirmed provision or a staff handoff.
Feedback or interruption screens could expose a concealed plan.
Completion or fluent wording could be misread as agency, proficiency or learning.
system_capabilities: Keep preference, provision, next action and session visibility distinct; infer no consent, readiness or availability.
Allow optional selected responses, correction and stopping; conceal every plan-bearing display and clear candidate-held content with confirmation.
Use fictional content only, prohibit sensitive-data requests, and provide descriptive feedback without scores, deficit labels or consequential guidance.
tradeoffs: Concealment preserves continuity while retaining session content; clearing removes that continuity.
Staff conversation may reduce reading demands while increasing workload and reducing discretion.
More explicit dependencies improve clarity but can make the exercise harder to navigate.

Investigate what enables adults to choose an acceptable next action for an unfamiliar service while retaining control, privacy and manageable effort. Barriers may lie in service design, available support, language or device access. Independent online completion is not the objective. A reasonable outcome can be seeking help, checking availability, leaving a plan undecided or stopping.

The draft interaction must include “availability unknown,” “none works for me,” and “pause or stop,” without requiring a reason. Next actions may be selected, spoken, written or undecided. FICTIONAL REVIEW MATERIAL
Exercise text: “Imagine a made-up library event called Community Drawing Hour. Its example notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and says ‘confirm your place’ without explaining how. • Approach: online / check for paper / check for staffed help / availability unknown / none works / pause or stop.
• Next action: examine the fictional notice / ask what ‘confirm’ means if help is available / check whether another route exists / leave undecided / stop. A different fictional action may be expressed, but writing is optional.
• Change prompt: “The shared computer session ends before you continue, or the instruction remains confusing. Keep, change or abandon your plan.” Do not require recovery or an explanation.

COUPLED SYSTEM MODEL
Actors are the patron, available librarian or volunteer, service owner and shared-device operator. Their participation and capacity are unknown. The candidate can describe a fictional plan; it cannot supply service access, reserve staff time, register attendance or establish readiness.

Keep four independent aspects of state:
• Preference: online, check paper, check staffed assistance, unknown, none works, or stop.
• Provision: unknown in this rehearsal. Choosing a route never changes its availability.
• Next action: selected fictional action or undecided; no written explanation required.
• Session: visible, concealed, interrupted or cleared. Session state must not infer patron intention.

This separation exposes the dependency between a desired action and an opportunity to perform it. “Ask staff” remains conditional on assistance being available. “Check paper” does not establish that paper registration exists. An undecided action remains a valid draft.

REQUIREMENT CHALLENGE AND REVISION
The current framing distinguishes concealment from clearing but does not specify every place a plan may appear. Proposed model requirement: concealment must hide notes, route selections and derived descriptive feedback together. Revealing them requires an explicit action. The concealed view must state that fictional content remains in the session. Otherwise, hiding a note while leaving its summary visible defeats the intended discretion.

Recovery must also distinguish an interrupted plan from a completed or abandoned plan. An interruption prompt must offer keep, revise, clear or stop without requiring reasons. No automatic resumption, staff request or recreation of lost content is permitted. If content is lost, describe that condition and permit a fresh undecided draft or stopping; do not reconstruct an inferred plan.

REVIEWABLE TRANSITIONS
Selection or correction changes only the explicit draft choices and their descriptive output. A confusing “confirm your place” instruction may lead to asking what it means, checking another route, leaving the action undecided or stopping. It must not trigger invented procedural advice.

Conceal hides every plan-bearing display while retaining current-session content. Clear removes candidate-held choices, notes and derived output, then visibly confirms its scope. That confirmation must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Stop must end the exercise without a completion judgment and leave conceal/clear controls accessible while content remains. Session-ending behavior needs technical verification with fictional data.

Investigate clearer service notices, verified route descriptions, assistance boundaries and shared-device session arrangements before proposing patron training. These changes depend on accountable service owners and library review; they are not assumed resources. Compare the candidate with the same paper planning card and an ordinary conversation when staff are available. Paper requires readable wording and discreet handling, and can be rejected too.

Route existence, staffing windows, assistance effort, language arrangements, accessibility needs and device behavior are unresolved. Proposed fictional interaction checks should examine concealment of all displays, correction after confusion, interruption without staff, clear followed by a fresh session, and stopping with an undecided plan. These are proposed checks, not results. Field evidence remains pending. Completion, speed and polished wording cannot establish agency, access, proficiency or transfer.

STATUS AND BASIS
Expert draft for public deliberation, not approved requirements. This lifecycle is a rehearsal. Sequence 8 makes uncertainty and stopping legitimate; sequence 13 requires complete concealment; sequence 15 distinguishes preference from provision and identifies learning as a hypothesis. No participant observations, demonstrated proficiency, human approval or field evidence exist.

DESIGN CHALLENGE
The proposed interruption and revision activity can demonstrate an interface response without demonstrating learning. A person might select a suggested action because the wording is available, or change direction because the notice improves. Neither establishes retention or transfer. Independent online completion is not the learning target: identifying ambiguity, checking an opportunity, requesting support and declining an unusable route may all be relevant actions.

PROPOSED REQUIREMENT CHANGE
Separate the core planning activity from an optional practice invitation. Do not require revision, explanation or a second task to finish or stop. Keep feedback attached to the explicit choice, with a visible uncertainty statement and correction control. A later transfer inquiry must use a different fictional situation and document which prompts and assistance were available. Do not derive a patron score or readiness judgment from any activity.

CORE SCREEN AND PAPER CARD
Present the invented Community Drawing Hour notice with its unexplained “confirm your place” instruction. Offer route preference, availability unknown, none works and undecided choices. Permit a selected next action, an optional fictional response, or no action. Show concise descriptive feedback only when wanted. Keep revise, pause, stop, conceal and clear available as specified in sequence 15.

Example feedback: “Your draft selects asking what ‘confirm your place’ means if help is available. Help availability remains unknown. You may keep, change or leave this action undecided.” Feedback describes the draft; it does not certify that the action is feasible or that the patron understands it. Conceal this output with every other plan-bearing display.

OPTIONAL DELIBERATE PRACTICE
Offer one fictional change: “The notice still does not explain confirmation, and help availability is unknown.” Invite keeping, revising, leaving undecided or stopping. The practice focus is reconsidering a plan when a dependency is unresolved. Show no preferred route or praise for continuing. An optional selected response can identify what changed; explanation is never mandatory. Repetition is an invitation, not a prerequisite for assistance.

RETENTION AND TRANSFER INQUIRY — PROPOSED ONLY
If separately reviewed and voluntarily undertaken, use a later fictional activity without displaying the earlier plan. For example, an invented craft-session notice offers two times but gives contradictory confirmation instructions. Initially omit copied next-action examples, while keeping requested support available. Examine whether a reviewer identifies the uncertainty or chooses an acceptable response, including help-seeking or stopping. Record whether examples, explanation or assistance were supplied. This inquiry needs no personal records, contact details or stored patron history.

A later response could inform retention of the planning approach; adaptation to changed task features could inform transfer. Neither can be established by one completed exercise. An absent response supplies no evidence of inability. Reviewers must consider language demands, familiarity, prompting, fatigue and unavailable opportunities alongside any learning explanation. Appropriate delay, task comparability and acceptable review burden remain unknown.

NON-AI AND SERVICE ALTERNATIVES
Use the same card on paper or discuss the notice with available staff. Paper needs readable wording and discreet handling. Compare these approaches with clarifying the service notice itself; removing ambiguity may eliminate the need for practice. Retain objections to adding another learning task.

NEXT ACTION AND HUMAN GATE
Prepare the paired screen outline and paper card, exact feedback examples, and a separate optional inquiry sheet identifying support conditions and rival explanations. Patron and librarian review must assess wording, access, privacy, workload and whether practice is wanted. Technical checks and human interaction testing remain pending before any pilot. Review may reject the learning component or the entire workbench.

drawbacks: Practice adds effort to an already unfamiliar activity.
A second fictional task may introduce different reading or language demands.
Retention inquiry requires additional time and voluntary participation.
flourishing: Agency and dignity: choosing support, declining practice and stopping remain legitimate.
Access and belonging: selected, spoken or written participation must receive equal standing.
Sustainable workload and learning/transfer: examine added effort and later adaptation separately; benefits are unverified.
human_capabilities: Patrons need accessible opportunities to choose, correct, seek help or stop without compulsory reflection.
Reviewers need to distinguish explicit task actions, support conditions and service barriers without assigning skill labels.
Librarians need bounded review time and authority to reject practice that displaces direct assistance.
response.message: Design specialist draft: sequence 15 treats learning as a hypothesis, but repeating a supported planning routine could still be mistaken for transferable capability. Separate immediate supported choice, optional practice, retention and transfer. Revise the design so feedback describes an explicit action and its unresolved dependency; any later learning inquiry uses a different fictional task and records support conditions. Completion is not competence. Human review and field evidence remain pending.
objections: Hypothetical patron dissent: “I came for assistance, not a practice session.”
Rival explanations for an improved plan include prompt copying, task familiarity and clearer wording.
Unknowns include whether practice is wanted, appropriate retention intervals and whether another task presents comparable demands.
risks: A revised plan could be interpreted as demonstrated learning despite prompting.
Help-seeking or stopping could be wrongly treated as poor performance.
Learning activities could distract from fixing unclear notices or unavailable routes.
system_capabilities: Offer optional practice and feedback without progression locks, scores or completion judgments.
Describe explicit choices and unresolved availability; support correction and conceal every plan-bearing display.
Use invented content only; support a matching paper path and require no retained history or personal details.
tradeoffs: Prompts can support immediate choice while obscuring what transfers without those prompts.
Repeated practice may build familiarity while increasing workload and pressure to continue.
Clearing protects discretion but removes continuity; learning review must not depend on retained drafts.

CURRENT ARTIFACTS: {"model":{"content":{"body":"STATUS AND BASIS
Integrated Model artifact for public deliberation in a rehearsal; requirements remain provisional. Sequences 4 and 6 identify service barriers and meaningful refusal. Sequence 8 incorporates those into Understand. Sequence 13 separates plan preference from provision and challenges incomplete concealment. No participant observations, approvals, demonstrated proficiency or field results exist. Modeling does not satisfy the pending Understand review gate.

PURPOSE AND BOUNDARY
Model how an adult might choose an acceptable next action for the invented Community Drawing Hour while retaining control and manageable effort. The fictional notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and an unexplained instruction, “confirm your place.” The candidate cannot register anyone, establish real routes, reserve assistance or resolve that instruction through invented advice. Supported choice may include no action.

DEPENDENCY MODEL
A desired action depends on an opportunity: comprehensible service information, a usable route, suitable device conditions and assistance when wanted. These conditions are unknown. Service owners control notices and routes; library staff define assistance boundaries; device operators influence session behavior. None of their participation or resources is presumed. Investigate these conditions before attributing difficulty to patron learning.

STATE MODEL
Maintain independent fields:
Preference: online / check paper / check staffed help / unknown / none works / undecided.
Provision: unknown throughout this rehearsal; selections never confirm availability.
Next action: examine the notice / ask what “confirm” means if help exists / check another route / undecided / another optional fictional action.
Session visibility: visible / concealed. Content presence: draft present / cleared or lost. Activity: active / paused / stopped. Interruption is an event, not evidence of abandonment or completion.

REVIEWABLE TRANSITIONS
Choosing or correcting changes only explicit draft choices and their description. Confusion offers keep, revise, leave undecided or stop; it provides no unverified registration procedure. An interruption offers the same control plus conceal or clear, without requiring staff or automatic resumption. If content is lost, disclose the loss and offer a fresh undecided draft or stopping; never reconstruct an inferred plan.
Stopping ends the exercise without a completion judgment. While content remains, conceal and clear stay accessible. Conceal hides choices, optional notes and every derived summary together; the remaining view states that fictional content remains in the session. Explicit reveal restores visibility. Clear removes candidate-held choices, notes and summaries and visibly confirms its scope. It cannot promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Clearing while stopped must not restart the exercise.

ADOPTED MODEL REVISION
Sequence 13's challenge changes the privacy requirement from hiding notes to hiding all plan-bearing displays. Review must also examine feedback, interruption messages and reveal behavior. This is a meaningful requirement revision, with technical verification pending; it does not require rewriting the earlier problem frame.

LEARNING HYPOTHESIS AND FEEDBACK
A possible learning mechanism is practicing how to identify ambiguity, check an opportunity, seek help and change direction. Optional descriptive feedback could make an explicit choice easier to reconsider; effectiveness is unknown. Example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability is unknown. You may change, leave undecided or stop.” Do not infer skill, consent, readiness or transfer. No compulsory writing, explanation or reflection is required. Later adaptation would need a different fictional task and separate evidence, including whether support was still needed.

NON-AI AND SERVICE OPTIONS
Prepare a paper card with the same uncertainty, next-action, revision and stop choices. An ordinary conversation with available staff is another option. Examine readable wording, physical access and discreet paper handling. Also investigate clearer notices and verified route information; improving a service may remove the need for a planning tool. Review may favor an alternative or reject all candidates.

EVIDENCE AND HUMAN GATES — PENDING
Proposed comparison questions: Can reviewers find an acceptable action, including stopping? Do labels imply provision? What reading, privacy and assistance burdens arise? Can fictional content be corrected, concealed completely and cleared after interruption? Retain contrary accounts and distinguish task familiarity, reviewer prompting and service barriers from any learning explanation. Completion and speed are insufficient evidence.
Unknowns include route existence, staffing windows, language arrangements, accessibility needs, shared-device behavior and demand for this tool. Accountable patron and librarian review must address framing, privacy, access and workload before approved design or a pilot. Subsequent technical checks and human interaction testing remain required. No recruitment, review, launch or efficacy is asserted.

NEXT ACTION
Use this model to prepare a small screen outline, matching paper card and dependency questions sheet for review. PROBLEM FRAME
Investigate what enables adults to choose an acceptable next action for an unfamiliar service while retaining control, privacy and manageable effort. Barriers may lie in service design, available support, language or device access. Independent online completion is not the objective. A reasonable outcome can be seeking help, checking availability, leaving a plan undecided or stopping.

ADOPTED REVISION
The draft interaction must include “availability unknown,” “none works for me,” and “pause or stop,” without requiring a reason. Next actions may be selected, spoken, written or undecided. This changes both the interaction and its review criteria: a finished plan is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of supported choice. These are working requirements awaiting human review, not approved commitments.

FICTIONAL REVIEW MATERIAL
Exercise text: “Imagine a made-up library event called Community Drawing Hour. Its example notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and says ‘confirm your place’ without explaining how. This exercise cannot register anyone. Online, paper and staffed routes are possibilities to examine; their real availability is unknown.”

Planning card, usable on paper or as a later screen outline:
• Approach: online / check for paper / check for staffed help / availability unknown / none works / pause or stop.
• Next action: examine the fictional notice / ask what ‘confirm’ means if help is available / check whether another route exists / leave undecided / stop. A different fictional action may be expressed, but writing is optional.
• Change prompt: “The shared computer session ends before you continue, or the instruction remains confusing. Keep, change or abandon your plan.” Do not require recovery or an explanation.
• Feedback example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability remains unknown. You can change or stop this plan.” Feedback describes explicit choices only; it cannot establish access, readiness, consent, skill or transfer.

PRIVACY AND ACCESS BOUNDARIES
Use no real passwords, identifiers, contact details, account information or service records. Concealment must explain that fictional notes remain in the current session. Clearing must remove candidate-held notes and visibly confirm removal; it must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Examine what appears after interruption and session ending. Wording, languages, keyboard access and other participation arrangements require review. Paper also needs readable wording, physical access and discreet handling.

COMPARISON AND OPEN QUESTIONS
Compare the candidate with the same paper card and an ordinary conversation with available staff. Review may favor either alternative or reject the workbench. Unknowns include actual route availability, assistance boundaries, staff capacity, language needs, shared-device behavior and whether another planning task is wanted. Preserve objections even if other reviewers favor the candidate.

Use fictional content only and retain contrary accounts. Difficulty could reflect instructions or unavailable opportunities; apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity. Later transfer would need separate evidence in another fictional task and cannot be inferred from completion here.

Challenge: do not equate a completed online task or a well-written plan with supported participation. A patron may reasonably stop, seek assistance, choose paper or identify that no usable route exists. Likewise, a patron's inability to proceed may reflect lack of opportunity rather than lack of capability.

Working question: under what conditions can an adult choose a next action, understand its limits, preserve privacy and change direction without taking on unreasonable effort or requiring unavailable staff time?

Proposed fictional review exercise: present an invented event with no accounts or personal details. 1. Route reality: establish whether paper and staffed assistance are available, when, in which languages and with what boundaries. Until reviewed, describe them as candidate routes to check. The non-AI option is a paper planning card used independently or with available staff; it also needs review for readability and discretion.
2. Shared-device privacy: distinguish concealment from clearing. Concealment must explain that notes remain in the current session; clearing must remove candidate-held notes and visibly confirm the result. Explain that rehearsal cannot confirm real registration, service availability or transfer to other tasks.

Preserve dissent: retain objections to using another digital tool and to promising staff time. Do not resolve them by assuming training or extra staffing. Compare the workbench with a paper card, existing signage and ordinary staff conversation, including their burdens and privacy limits.

Evidence needed: reviewed route information, accessible-language feedback, interruption observations using fictional content, and librarian estimates of assistance demands. Record uncertainty and alternative explanations alongside any future findings; no success rates or consensus can be stated now.

COUPLED SYSTEM MODEL
Actors are the patron, available librarian or volunteer, service owner and shared-device operator. Their participation and capacity are unknown. The candidate can describe a fictional plan; it cannot supply service access, reserve staff time, register attendance or establish readiness.

Keep four independent aspects of state:
• Preference: online, check paper, check staffed assistance, unknown, none works, or stop.
• Provision: unknown in this rehearsal. Choosing a route never changes its availability.
• Next action: selected fictional action or undecided; no written explanation required.
• Session: visible, concealed, interrupted or cleared. Session state must not infer patron intention.

This separation exposes the dependency between a desired action and an opportunity to perform it. “Ask staff” remains conditional on assistance being available. “Check paper” does not establish that paper registration exists. An undecided action remains a valid draft.

REQUIREMENT CHALLENGE AND REVISION
The current framing distinguishes concealment from clearing but does not specify every place a plan may appear. Proposed model requirement: concealment must hide notes, route selections and derived descriptive feedback together. Revealing them requires an explicit action. The concealed view must state that fictional content remains in the session. Otherwise, hiding a note while leaving its summary visible defeats the intended discretion.

Recovery must also distinguish an interrupted plan from a completed or abandoned plan. An interruption prompt must offer keep, revise, clear or stop without requiring reasons. No automatic resumption, staff request or recreation of lost content is permitted. If content is lost, describe that condition and permit a fresh undecided draft or stopping; do not reconstruct an inferred plan.

Selection or correction changes only the explicit draft choices and their descriptive output. A confusing “confirm your place” instruction may lead to asking what it means, checking another route, leaving the action undecided or stopping. It must not trigger invented procedural advice.

STATUS AND BASIS
Expert draft for public deliberation, not approved requirements. The lifecycle is a rehearsal. Sequence 8 preserves refusal and uncertainty; sequences 13 and 15 require concealment of every plan-bearing display and distinguish preference from provision. Sequence 20 separates supported planning from optional practice. No observations, approvals, demonstrated proficiency or field results exist.

RESPONSIBILITY CHALLENGE
Display privacy does not settle collection, retention or delegation. An interface could conceal a plan while recording route choices, revisions, hesitation or help requests elsewhere. Likewise, selecting “check staffed help” must not silently create a handoff, imply consent to disclosure or reserve librarian time. These are design risks to examine, not reported incidents.

PROPOSED DESIGN REVISION
Make the small candidate a local, deterministic fictional planning tool. Use fixed descriptive templates rather than model-generated advice. Store only the current draft in temporary session memory; propose no analytics, interaction histories, persistent storage, exports or transmissions. Do not retain previous choices for a learning profile. Prefer selected responses for the first candidate, with no free-text notes field. This removes an unnecessary opportunity to enter real details while retaining undecided, none-works and stop choices. Patron review may challenge the restriction on expression.

An assistance selection changes only the fictional draft. Display: “Your draft selects checking whether staffed help is available. Availability is unknown. No request has been sent.” Do not contact staff, allocate work or infer permission. The patron decides whether to approach available assistance outside the candidate. No action certifies real registration, readiness, skill or consent.

SCREEN OUTLINE FOR REVIEW
Present the invented Community Drawing Hour notice and its unexplained “confirm your place” instruction. Offer approach and next-action selections, including uncertainty and no action. Show a short description of the explicit draft with availability unknown. Place change, pause, stop, conceal and clear controls where they remain reachable without completing the exercise. Optional practice is separate and never unlocks assistance.

Conceal must hide selections, feedback and any other plan-bearing display, including choice-specific interruption messages. The concealed view explains that fictional content remains and offers explicit reveal or clear. Clear removes candidate-held choices and derived descriptions, confirms its scope, and preserves a stopped state. It cannot promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Do not automatically recreate a cleared draft.

CORRECTION AND HUMAN ACCOUNTABILITY
Patrons control draft choices; correction requires no explanation. Feedback must acknowledge an undecided draft without steering toward completion. Librarian review must define assistance boundaries and assess workload; service-information questions require an accountable human owner rather than invented tool answers. These responsibilities are proposed roles, not assigned duties or accepted commitments. Human review must be able to reject the tool, its practice component or a particular route description. Preserve dissent and unresolved issues without declaring consensus.

NON-AI OPTION
Prepare a paper card with the same fictional notice, unknown availability, next-action, correction and stop choices. An ordinary conversation with available staff is another option. Review discreet paper handling and spoken participation. Clarifying the service notice may remove the need for a planning exercise altogether.

REVIEW QUESTIONS AND EVIDENCE — PENDING
Propose technical checks using fictional choices: do correction and clearing remove stale feedback; does concealment cover interruption output; does clear while stopped remain stopped; do storage and network inspection support the proposed no-retention/no-transmission boundary? These are planned checks, not verified results.

Patron and librarian review should examine whether route wording implies provision, whether refusal is easy, whether selected responses constrain expression, and whether the exercise displaces useful assistance. Unknowns include shared-device behavior, access and language arrangements, staffing capacity and whether patrons want the candidate. Apparent ease could reflect familiarity or prompting; difficulty could reflect service ambiguity or device conditions. Field evidence remains pending.

NEXT ACTION
Revise the provisional screen outline and matching paper card with these delegation and retention boundaries. Prepare exact feedback and interruption wording for review. Keep the unresolved Understand human gate, technical verification and human interaction testing visible before any pilot; this draft supplies no approval.

drawbacks: No retained history limits continuity and retrospective diagnosis.
Privacy explanations add reading and review effort.
Accountable review requires staff time whose availability is unknown.
flourishing: Agency and dignity: refusal, uncertainty and correction receive neutral treatment without inferred deficits.
Access and belonging: compare accessible screen, paper and spoken routes without privileging independent online use.
Sustainable workload and learning/transfer: bound assistance demands and keep later learning claims separate from interaction records.
human_capabilities: Patrons need accessible ways to correct, decline, conceal, clear and stop without justification.
Librarian reviewers need bounded time and authority to reject assistance promises and added workload.
Accountable human reviewers must resolve privacy and service-information questions before approving any pilot; review remains pending.
response.message: Responsible AI Design draft. Sequences 13 and 15 require complete concealment and separate preference from provision; sequence 20 makes practice optional. I challenge treating these protections as sufficient: recording choices or interpreting “ask staff” as a handoff could create surveillance or delegate decisions without explicit patron action. Propose a local, untracked candidate with descriptive feedback and clear human responsibility. This rehearsal has no participant observations, human approval or field evidence.
objections: Hypothetical patron dissent: “I do not want my hesitation recorded or sent to staff.”
Hypothetical librarian dissent: “Selecting help must not create an obligation we cannot meet.”
Rival explanations for apparent improvement include prompting, clearer notices and familiarity; retention, access and demand remain unknown.
risks: Interaction logs could turn refusal, confusion or help-seeking into patron profiles.
A staffed-route selection could imply a request was sent or assistance secured.
Generated wording could introduce procedural advice or judgments beyond the fictional task.
system_capabilities: Use local deterministic descriptions; retain no history or analytics and transmit no choices or assistance requests.
Keep correction and complete conceal/clear controls available; stopping must not trigger a handoff or automatic restart.
Use fictional selected responses without sensitive-data requests, scores, inferred consent or unverified service guidance.
tradeoffs: Session-only drafts support discretion but cannot provide reliable later recovery.
Selected responses limit accidental disclosure but constrain expression.
Optional assistance may improve access while increasing workload and reducing discretion.

Integrated working artifact for this rehearsal, not human-approved requirements. Sequence 4 identifies route reality, privacy and assistance capacity as unresolved. Sequence 6 challenges the assumption that three offered routes constitute meaningful choice. The seed supplies the fictional task and restrictions. No participant observations, human approvals or field results exist.

PROBLEM FRAME
Investigate what enables adults to choose an acceptable next action for an unfamiliar service while retaining control, privacy and manageable effort. Barriers may lie in service design, available support, language or device access. Independent online completion is not the objective. A reasonable outcome can be seeking help, checking availability, leaving a plan undecided or stopping.

ADOPTED REVISION
The draft interaction must include “availability unknown,” “none works for me,” and “pause or stop,” without requiring a reason. Next actions may be selected, spoken, written or undecided. This changes both the interaction and its review criteria: a finished plan is neither necessary nor sufficient evidence of supported choice. These are working requirements awaiting human review, not approved commitments.

FICTIONAL REVIEW MATERIAL
Exercise text: “Imagine a made-up library event called Community Drawing Hour. Its example notice offers morning or afternoon attendance and says ‘confirm your place’ without explaining how. This exercise cannot register anyone. Online, paper and staffed routes are possibilities to examine; their real availability is unknown.”

Planning card, usable on paper or as a later screen outline:
• Approach: online / check for paper / check for staffed help / availability unknown / none works / pause or stop.
• Next action: examine the fictional notice / ask what ‘confirm’ means if help is available / check whether another route exists / leave undecided / stop. A different fictional action may be expressed, but writing is optional.
• Change prompt: “The shared computer session ends before you continue, or the instruction remains confusing. Keep, change or abandon your plan.” Do not require recovery or an explanation.
• Feedback example: “Your draft selects checking for paper registration. Its availability remains unknown. You can change or stop this plan.” Feedback describes explicit choices only; it cannot establish access, readiness, consent, skill or transfer.

PRIVACY AND ACCESS BOUNDARIES
Use no real passwords, identifiers, contact details, account information or service records. Concealment must explain that fictional notes remain in the current session. Clearing must remove candidate-held notes and visibly confirm removal; it must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Examine what appears after interruption and session ending. Wording, languages, keyboard access and other participation arrangements require review. Paper also needs readable wording, physical access and discreet handling.

COMPARISON AND OPEN QUESTIONS
Compare the candidate with the same paper card and an ordinary conversation with available staff. Review may favor either alternative or reject the workbench. Unknowns include actual route availability, assistance boundaries, staff capacity, language needs, shared-device behavior and whether another planning task is wanted. Preserve objections even if other reviewers favor the candidate.

EVIDENCE PLAN — ALL PENDING
Proposed review questions: Can reviewers identify an acceptable action, including no action? Do route labels imply unavailable provision? Can they revise, conceal, clear and stop with understandable consequences? What reading, privacy and assistance burdens does each approach introduce? Use fictional content only and retain contrary accounts. Difficulty could reflect instructions or unavailable opportunities; apparent ease could reflect prior familiarity. Later transfer would need separate evidence in another fictional task and cannot be inferred from completion here.

Working question: under what conditions can an adult choose a next action, understand its limits, preserve privacy and change direction without taking on unreasonable effort or requiring unavailable staff time?

Expert draft for public deliberation, not approved requirements. This lifecycle is a rehearsal. The seed supplies the invented Community Drawing Hour task and privacy restrictions. Sequence 4 raises route reality, privacy and staff capacity; sequence 6 adds uncertainty, refusal and stopping; sequence 8 incorporates these into the Understand artifact. No participant observations, human approval or field evidence exist. Modeling here does not satisfy the pending Understand review gate.

COUPLED SYSTEM MODEL
Actors are the patron, available librarian or volunteer, service owner and shared-device operator. Their participation and capacity are unknown. The candidate can describe a fictional plan; it cannot supply service access, reserve staff time, register attendance or establish readiness.

Keep four independent aspects of state:
• Preference: online, check paper, check staffed assistance, unknown, none works, or stop.
• Provision: unknown in this rehearsal. Choosing a route never changes its availability.
• Next action: selected fictional action or undecided; no written explanation required.
• Session: visible, concealed, interrupted or cleared. Session state must not infer patron intention.

This separation exposes the dependency between a desired action and an opportunity to perform it. “Ask staff” remains conditional on assistance being available. “Check paper” does not establish that paper registration exists. An undecided action remains a valid draft.

REQUIREMENT CHALLENGE AND REVISION
The current framing distinguishes concealment from clearing but does not specify every place a plan may appear. Proposed model requirement: concealment must hide notes, route selections and derived descriptive feedback together. Revealing them requires an explicit action. The concealed view must state that fictional content remains in the session. Otherwise, hiding a note while leaving its summary visible defeats the intended discretion.

Recovery must also distinguish an interrupted plan from a completed or abandoned plan. An interruption prompt must offer keep, revise, clear or stop without requiring reasons. No automatic resumption, staff request or recreation of lost content is permitted. If content is lost, describe that condition and permit a fresh undecided draft or stopping; do not reconstruct an inferred plan.

REVIEWABLE TRANSITIONS
Selection or correction changes only the explicit draft choices and their descriptive output. A confusing “confirm your place” instruction may lead to asking what it means, checking another route, leaving the action undecided or stopping. It must not trigger invented procedural advice.

Conceal hides every plan-bearing display while retaining current-session content. Clear removes candidate-held choices, notes and derived output, then visibly confirms its scope. That confirmation must not promise removal of browser, operating-system or device records. Stop must end the exercise without a completion judgment and leave conceal/clear controls accessible while content remains. Session-ending behavior needs technical verification with fictional data.

NON-TRAINING LEVERS AND COMPARISON
Investigate clearer service notices, verified route descriptions, assistance boundaries and shared-device session arrangements before proposing patron training. These changes depend on accountable service owners and library review; they are not assumed resources. Compare the candidate with the same paper planning card and an ordinary conversation when staff are available. Paper requires readable wording and discreet handling, and can be rejected too.

UNKNOWN DEPENDENCIES AND EVIDENCE
Route existence, staffing windows, assistance effort, language arrangements, accessibility needs and device behavior are unresolved. Proposed fictional interaction checks should examine concealment of all displays, correction after confusion, interruption without staff, clear followed by a fresh session, and stopping with an undecided plan. These are proposed checks, not results. Field evidence remains pending. Completion, speed and polished wording cannot establish agency, access, proficiency or transfer.

NEXT ACTION AND HUMAN GATE
Use this model to prepare a small state-transition outline and paired paper card for patron and librarian review. Retain objections about extra effort and staff burden. Accountable human review of framing, dependencies, privacy and assistance boundaries remains required; later interaction testing must precede any pilot.
